t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: For which concepts does Place think a behavioral-disposition analysis (à la Ryle and Wittgenstein) is fundamentally sound?
a: Cognitive and volitional ones, like believing
w: Sensations and mental imagery, like after-images
Every mental concept without any exception
None, since he rejects behaviorism entirely
e: Cognitive and volitional concepts like knowing, believing, wanting, intending. For consciousness, experience, sensation and imagery there's an 'intractable residue' where an inner-process story is unavoidable.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: Place's status claim for 'consciousness is a process in the brain' is that it is:
w: True by definition of the words
A logically necessary truth
Logically impossible to state
e: A reasonable scientific hypothesis: neither self-contradictory nor self-evident. Just as 'lightning is a motion of electric charges' is a reasonable scientific hypothesis.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: Place denies that statements about sensations MEAN statements about brain processes. Which reason does he give?
a: You can describe sensations knowing nothing of brains
w: Brains don't exist as separate objects at all
Sensations are immaterial and can't be in the brain
Neuroscience is still too incomplete to tell
e: You can describe your sensations without knowing anything about your brain. Also, the two kinds of statement are verified differently, and 'X has a pain but nothing's going on in his brain' isn't self-contradictory.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: 'His table is an old packing case' is an example of the:
w: 'Is' of definition
'Is' of predication
'Is' of existence
e: 'Is' of composition: contingent, verified by observation. Contrast 'a square is an equilateral rectangle', the 'is' of definition. Place says consciousness = brain process uses the 'is' of composition.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: What test does Place say distinguishes definition/composition 'is' statements from predication?
a: You can sensibly add 'and nothing else'
w: They can be verified by introspection
They contain a proper name
They are always false
e: 'Her hat is a bundle of straw and nothing else' makes sense. 'Her hat is red and nothing else' is nonsense.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: Place says we're normally justified in inferring ontological independence from logical independence of expressions, but this breaks down when:
a: The two kinds of observation can't be made together
w: The objects involved are extremely small in size
The two expressions are actually exact synonyms
One of the two objects described is purely fictional
e: The observations verifying each description can seldom if ever be performed simultaneously. Example: you can't observe a cloud's fleecy shape and its microstructure at once. Up close, a cloud becomes 'fog' or 'mist'.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: In Place's cloud example, what happens to the cloud when you're enveloped by it?
a: We call it a fog or mist
w: It disappears entirely
It becomes a solid
It turns into lightning
e: The experiences are so different we use different words, yet there's only one thing: a mass of tiny particles.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: Why does Place need the lightning example in addition to the cloud?
a: Lightning, unlike a cloud, has no continuous approach
w: Lightning is much easier to see than clouds are
Clouds turn out not to be physical things after all
Lightning is really a kind of mental event, like pain
e: In the cloud case observations are continuous as you approach; lightning, like consciousness, has no such continuity. Introspection will never reveal nerve impulses, just as staring at lightning never reveals electric charges.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: Tides and phases of the moon are systematically correlated. Why don't we say they're the same event?
w: They aren't actually correlated
The moon is far too distant
Tides are partly mental events
e: The moon causes the tides, not our observations of tidal measurements. We identify two sets of observations when the scientific account directly explains the ordinary observations.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: Place's criterion for treating two sets of observations as observations of the same event is that:
a: The science immediately explains the everyday observations
w: The two sets of observations are perfectly correlated
Both sets of observations occur at exactly the same time
Both sets of observations are described with the same words
e: The scientific observations, in context of theory, provide an immediate explanation of the everyday observations. Moving charges explain why observers report a flash. So we identify consciousness with brain processes if brain processes explain introspective reports.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: Sherrington's worry about the brain producing the 'seen' sun involves vision's strange property of:
w: Inversion
Divisibility
Multiple realizability
e: Projection: what's seen seems to be at a distance from the seeing self. Sherrington concluded there are two series of events, physico-chemical and psychical.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: The 'phenomenological fallacy' is the mistake of thinking that describing your experience means:
a: Describing objects on an inner 'mental screen'
w: Describing the physical processes in your brain
Describing your outward behavior and dispositions
Saying nothing at all, since it's meaningless
e: Describing literal properties of objects on an internal 'phenomenal field' (a mental cinema screen). E.g., thinking a green after-image is a literally green object inside you, which has no place in physics.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: According to Place, when you say your after-image is green, you're really saying:
a: It's like the experience of seeing a green patch
w: There is a small green object inside your brain
There is a green object out in front of you
Your brain is giving off a faint green light
e: You're having the sort of experience you normally have when looking at a green patch of light. We learn to describe real things first, and describe experience by reference to them, not the reverse.

t: Place – Is Consciousness a Brain Process?
q: To explain introspection physiologically, Place says we need to explain how a subject learns to:
a: Say 'it seems' or 'it looks' when appropriate
w: See directly inside their own brain as it works
Stop describing their experiences altogether
Translate each experience into outward behavior
e: Preface ordinary descriptions with 'it appears', 'seems', 'looks' when they may not be appropriate. E.g., a stationary light that appears to move: the brain process is the kind that normally occurs when seeing an actual moving object.
